subject: Spatially varying coefficients using an approach other than 'besag' (CAR) model

messages.author: d07cf6c199aec725
messages.subject: Spatially varying coefficients using an approach other than 'besag' (CAR) model
parts:
Hi All,

I am curious if it is possible to fit a spatially varying coefficients model using an approach other than a CAR model (model = 'besag' in INLA) in INLA?

For example, I have created a mesh surface here:

coords <- as.matrix(DF[, 1:2])

prdomain <- inla.nonconvex.hull(coords)

prmesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = prdomain, max.edge = c(25, 50), cutoff = 5)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(prmesh, loc = coords)

spde <- inla.spde2.matern(prmesh, alpha = 2)

w.index = inla.spde.make.index(
  name = 'w',
  n.spde = spde$n.spde,
  n.group = 1,
  n.repl = 1)

And then I can add a spatial random effect like so:

y ~ -1 + Intercept + vegetation + f(w, model = spde)

From the examples that I have seen, to get the spatially varying coefficient users will then apply something like this:

f(index, vegetation, model = 'besag', graph = g)

My question is whether it is possible to use my spde object from above to get an estimate of the variation in the effect of, say, vegetation across that surface? something like:

f(w, vegetation, model = spde)


If the last f() is nonsense, are there any other ways with INLA to get a spatially varying coefficient? I do know how to code random intercepts and slopes in INLA, but I am hoping to get something spatially explicit. 

Thanks for your time,
Brent

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatially varying coefficients using an approach other than 'besag' (CAR) model
parts:
Hi,
Yes, you can specify such a model in several ways. When using spde models in inla, one tends to use inla.stack() constructions, and then one can include the covariate, vegetation in your case in the A matrix for evaluating the field.

There are three main cases:
1) the covariate is known at the observed points.
2) the covariate is known on a grid
3) the covariate is known on the mesh nodes

If one wants to do prediction, case 2 or 3 are required.

The suggestions below all use f(w, model=spde) in the inla formula, and introduce the covariate multiplication in the A matrix in an inla.stack() call.

In case 1, let A be the A matrix for evaluating the field on the mesh (please refer to the extensive case studies and examples on r-inla.org for details on this.
Let veg be the vector of vegetation values for each observation.
Then you need to use
  Diagonal(length(veg), veg) %*% A
as the A matrix in the inla.stack call instead of just A.

In case 3, let veg be the vector of vegetation values for each mesh node.
Then you need to use
  A %*% Diagonal(length(veg), veg)
as the A matrix.

In case 2, in the past I’ve used a preprocessing step to map the covariate onto the mesh first, and then proceed as in case 3.
Nowadays I would use the inlabru interface instead, where one old define a function of the coordinates to evaluate the covariate at arbitrary locations, and construct the desired multiplication in the model formula, as
  veg(x,y) * field

Finn

parts:
Thank you for the response, Finn, that was very helpful. A few follow ups:

I am indeed using a inla.stack(). It looks something like this:

StackFit <- inla.stack(
  tag = 'Fit',
  data = list(y = df$Y),
  A = list(1,1,1,1,A),
  effects = list(
    Index = seq(1, nrow(df),1),
    Intercept = rep(1,nrow(df)),
    X = X,
    effort = df$effort,
    w = w.index))

Then here is the example model:
  form <- y ~ -1 + Intercept + vegetation + offset(effort) + f(w, model = spde)
1 model1 <- inla(form, family = 'poisson',
2           control.compute = list(
3             waic = T,
4             cpo = T,
5             dic = T),
6           num.threads = 8,
7           data = inla.stack.data(StackFit),
8           control.predictor = list(
9             A = inla.stack.A(StackFit)))

For case one, are you suggesting that in line 9 of the inla() above I replace the "A = inla.stack.A(StackFit)" with "A = Diagonal(length(veg), veg) %*% A"? Or does the "Diagonal...%*% A" need to be done somewhere within the creation of StackFit?


Thanks again for your help!

f(index, vegetation, model = 'besag', graph = g)

My question is whether it is possible to use my spde object from above to get an estimate of the variation in the effect of, say, vegetation across that surface? something like:

f(w, vegetation, model = spde)


If the last f() is nonsense, are there any other ways with INLA to get a spatially varying coefficient? I do know how to code random intercepts and slopes in INLA, but I am hoping to get something spatially explicit. 

Thanks for your time,
Brent
